tasks.prompt: STAR #3 full take, timed 2 minutes (S-T-A-R, Result as point → reason → example). Then answer the follow-up aloud: 'The direction kept changing. What did you do?' Check against the script after.
tasks.script: On an AI data-centre policy research programme, I was the sole analyst. The scope was ambiguous: there was no agreed definition of an 'AI data centre', the public data on energy, water, cooling, cost and land use was fragmented, and the project direction changed quite often. (S) My task was to build a defensible evidence base and policy analysis, even though the requirements were unclear and I had no one to review my work. (T) First, I pushed for a working definition of what counts as an AI data centre, so the whole analysis was built on the same scope. Second, I mapped the data gaps: I counted which indicators Hong Kong was missing and compared them with other governments and regions. Third, because the direction kept shifting, I built an iterative research workflow, so I could update the analysis step by step without starting again. And after every meeting, I kept a written log of what we agreed: the direction, the deliverables and the deadlines. (A) As a result, I delivered a baseline analysis of data-centre governance from an international perspective. That matters because it gives future policy work a clear starting point. For example, the gap list showed exactly which indicators Hong Kong still needs to collect. (R) Looking back, confirming the scope early and keeping a written record protects both quality and timelines. || Follow-up (changing direction): When the direction changed, I updated the workflow step by step instead of starting again. I focused on what we had agreed, not on who changed it.
